---
title: "How much did unemployment rise as inflation fell after 2022?"
description: "Most of the fall in inflation came before the clearer rise in unemployment."
author: "Yipin Zhang"
date: 2026-10-01
date-modified: 2026-10-06
categories: [inflation, unemployment, data visualization]
image: results/figures/path.png
execute:
  freeze: false
  cache: false
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
here::i_am("posts/inflation-unemployment/index.qmd")
POST_DIR <- here::here("posts", "inflation-unemployment")
a <- readRDS(file.path(POST_DIR, "results/analysis.rds"))
f <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", x)
date_label <- function(x) format(x, "%B %Y")
qval <- function(label, variable) a$quarterly[[variable]][a$quarterly$label == label]
point <- function(date, variable) a$monthly[[variable]][a$monthly$date == as.Date(date)]
provenance <- read.csv(file.path(POST_DIR, "data/raw/provenance.csv"))
```

Slower price increases bring relief to household budgets, but that relief can feel less reassuring if jobs become harder to find. Did the fall in U.S. inflation after 2022 come with a large rise in unemployment? And did that rise happen throughout the slowdown in inflation, or mainly toward the end?

These questions relate to the [Phillips curve](https://www.stlouisfed.org/publications/page-one-economics/2021/07/15/inflation-expectations-the-phillips-curve-and-the-feds-dual-mandate), a framework for thinking about inflation and unemployment. A concern is that cooling demand to slow price increases could also weaken hiring. The recent experience offers a useful comparison, although the charts alone cannot tell us what caused either rate to change.

I compare monthly U.S. unemployment with consumer price inflation using Bureau of Labor Statistics data available through FRED. Both series are seasonally adjusted. Inflation measures how much prices increased compared with the same month a year earlier, while unemployment measures the share of the labor force without work and looking for a job. Falling inflation therefore means prices rise more slowly, not that prices fall.

The first chart shows why timing matters. Inflation peaked at `r f(a$peak$inflation)`% in `r date_label(a$peak$date)`, when unemployment was `r f(a$peak$UNRATE)`%. By `r date_label(a$end$date)`, inflation had fallen to `r f(a$end$inflation)`%, while unemployment had risen to `r f(a$end$UNRATE)`%. Across those endpoints, inflation fell `r f(a$peak$inflation - a$end$inflation)` percentage points and unemployment rose `r f(a$end$UNRATE - a$peak$UNRATE)` points.

```{r}
#| label: fig-timeline
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Monthly rates on a common scale. The dotted line marks the inflation peak; points label that peak, the subsequent unemployment trough, and December 2024."
#| fig-alt: "Inflation peaks in June 2022, while unemployment reaches its subsequent low in April 2023 before rising."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(POST_DIR, "results/figures/timeline.png"))
```

That comparison misses an important turn along the way. Unemployment initially continued falling, reaching `r f(a$trough$UNRATE)`% in `r date_label(a$trough$date)`. From that low to December 2024, it rose `r f(a$end$UNRATE - a$trough$UNRATE)` points. The smaller increase measures change since peak inflation; the larger one captures the subsequent weakening from the strongest labor market reading. Both describe the same episode, but answer different questions.

To understand why we should not expect a fixed exchange between the two rates, the second chart puts this episode in a longer context. Each point pairs inflation and unemployment in one month. It distinguishes 2015 through 2019 before COVID, the disruption in 2020 and 2021, and the inflation and cooling period from 2022 through 2024.

```{r}
#| label: fig-scatter
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Each point represents one month. Calendar groups provide historical context and are not estimated structural breaks."
#| fig-alt: "A scatterplot shows different inflation rates at similar unemployment levels across the three calendar periods."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(POST_DIR, "results/figures/scatter.png"))
```

Unemployment was `r f(point("2019-12-01", "UNRATE"))`% in December 2019 and `r f(point("2022-06-01", "UNRATE"))`% in June 2022. Yet inflation was `r f(point("2019-12-01", "inflation"))`% in the first month and `r f(point("2022-06-01", "inflation"))`% in the second. Similar unemployment accompanied very different inflation. Unemployment alone does not explain the price pressures households faced.

The final chart returns to the recent episode and connects the observations in time. Each point averages three months to make the path easier to follow. Moving downward means inflation fell; moving right means unemployment rose. Its unemployment axis is narrower than the previous chart's, so distances should not be compared across the two figures.

```{r}
#| label: fig-path
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Arrows follow consecutive quarters. Quarterly inflation is the mean of monthly annual inflation rates, not an annualized quarterly growth rate."
#| fig-alt: "A quarterly path shows substantial initial inflation declines with little unemployment movement, followed by rising unemployment and smaller further inflation declines."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(POST_DIR, "results/figures/path.png"))
```

Much of the initial movement was downward. From `r a$start_q$label` to `r a$split_q$label`, inflation fell from `r f(a$start_q$inflation)`% to `r f(a$split_q$inflation)`%, while unemployment stayed close to `r f(a$split_q$unemployment)`%. I use the latter quarter because it was the first to complete at least half the inflation decline through the end of 2024. This is a descriptive comparison, not evidence of a permanent change in the relationship.

Afterward, the path moved more clearly to the right. By 2024 Q4, unemployment averaged `r f(qval("2024 Q4", "unemployment"))`% and inflation `r f(qval("2024 Q4", "inflation"))`%. The broad contrast matters more than movements of a tenth of a point, which should be interpreted cautiously given the survey's sampling uncertainty.

The episode does not resemble a fixed Phillips curve tradeoff in which every point of lower inflation requires a corresponding rise in unemployment. It also does not establish that reducing inflation is always painless. Supply conditions, demand, expectations, and policy can all affect these outcomes, and national averages conceal different experiences across households.

The main takeaways are

* Much of the fall in inflation came before the clearer rise in unemployment.
* Unemployment rose by `r f(a$end$UNRATE - a$peak$UNRATE)` percentage points from peak inflation, or `r f(a$end$UNRATE - a$trough$UNRATE)` points from its subsequent low. The starting date matters.
* These comparisons describe what happened, rather than the effects of a particular policy.

Data come from BLS via FRED's [consumer price index](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CPIAUCSL) and [unemployment rate](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/UNRATE). The [GitHub repository](https://github.com/yipin-grena/aeds6400-blog/tree/main/posts/inflation-unemployment) contains the data, code, methods, and instructions for reproducing the analysis.
